sections.summary: One of the seven bowl-angels invites John to see the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed immorality and whose wine intoxicated the earth-dwellers, drawing on the prophetic tradition of Jeremiah 51:7 and Ezekiel 16 to characterize the harlot-city's seductive political-religious alliances.

sections.section_title: The Woman on the Scarlet Beast in the Wilderness
sections.summary: John is transported in the Spirit to a wilderness where he sees a woman seated on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, the same beast configuration as chapters 12-13, with the wilderness setting forming a deliberate contrast to the faithful woman of chapter 12 who was nourished in the wilderness as a place of refuge.

The harlot is clothed in purple and scarlet and adorned with gold, precious stones, and pearls -- a counterfeit of priestly splendor lacking the blue of the tabernacle's heavenly dimension -- holding a golden cup full of abominations, and bearing on her forehead the name 'Babylon the Great, the Mother of Harlots and of the Abominations of the Earth.'

The harlot is drunk with the blood of the saints and the witnesses of Jesus, revealing that her luxury is built on the murder of the faithful, and John marvels greatly at the sight -- a response the angel will immediately correct, since 'wondering' at the beast system is the precursor to being deceived by it.

sections.section_title: The Angel's Interpretation Begins -- The Mystery of the Beast
sections.summary: The angel begins interpreting the vision: the beast 'was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction' -- a deliberate parody of the divine self-identification 'who is and who was and who is to come' -- and those whose names have not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world will wonder at the beast's apparent conquest of death.
sections.relevance: Revelation 17:8 is a conventional proof-text for divine predetermination of salvation, since it states that earth-dwellers who marvel at the beast are specifically those 'whose name has not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world' (apo katabolēs kosmou). The pre-temporal registration implies a division between the faithful and the beast's followers that was established before human history. The neutral reading, however, frames this phrase pastorally rather than as a metaphysical argument about predetermination: 'The phrase functions pastorally: the faithful are not newly or tenuously inscribed but have been known to God since the beginning.' The passage's actual argument is about the beast as a counterfeit of divine eternity and about the earth-dwellers' susceptibility to that counterfeit -- the book of life reference serves to characterize who is deceived and who is not, rather than to explain the mechanism by which the distinction was established. The deterministic implication is genuine (pre-temporal registration correlates with present response to the beast), but the passage does not directly argue about who determines salvation outcomes; it assumes the distinction and uses it descriptively within the beast-parody argument.
key_phrases: those who dwell on the earth, whose name has not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world
will wonder when they see the beast, that he was and is not and will come
the beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction

sections.summary: The angel identifies the seven heads as seven mountains (pointing unmistakably to Rome) and seven kings distributed across three temporal categories -- five fallen, one present, one yet to come for a brief reign -- with the beast itself being an 'eighth' who is 'one of the seven' and whose trajectory terminates in destruction, likely evoking the Nero redivivus expectation as the vehicle for the theological point that the beast's power is a parody of God's eternal existence.

sections.section_title: The Ten Horns Interpreted -- Kings Who Wage War on the Lamb
sections.summary: The ten horns are ten future kings who receive authority with the beast for one brief hour, voluntarily surrender their power to the beast, and wage war against the Lamb -- but the Lamb overcomes them because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those with him are identified as 'the called and chosen and faithful.'
sections.relevance: The threefold identification of the Lamb's companions as 'the called and chosen and faithful' (klētoi kai eklektoi kai pistoi) is significant for the determinism question because of both its content and its sequence. The neutral reading explicitly notes: 'The order is significant: called first (God's initiative), chosen second (God's purpose), faithful third (the human response). The sequence moves from divine action to human fidelity.' Both divine initiative and human response are presented as genuinely operative. The reading further states that 'their inclusion among the Lamb's companions is confirmed by their faithfulness -- they responded to the call and fulfilled the purpose of their election by enduring.' The text does not present calling and choosing as sufficient by themselves to place someone among the Lamb's companions; faithfulness -- active, persevering human fidelity -- is the validating third element. The neutral reading also identifies eklektoi in its broader scriptural context as 'primarily corporate and vocational -- God chooses a people for a purpose (service, witness, being a light to the nations), not merely individuals for personal salvation.' The passage leans libertarian because it presents human faithfulness as a genuine and necessary response that confirms one's place among the Lamb's people, rather than treating the outcome as settled by calling and choosing alone.
key_phrases: those who are with him are the called and chosen and faithful
the Lamb will overcome them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings
they responded to the call and fulfilled the purpose of their election by enduring

sections.section_title: The Waters, the Horns' Betrayal, and the Woman Identified
sections.summary: The angel interprets the waters as peoples, multitudes, nations, and tongues; reveals that the ten horns and the beast will turn on the harlot and destroy her through hatred, stripping, devouring, and burning -- a betrayal that is not random but divinely orchestrated ('God has put it in their hearts to execute his purpose') until God's words are fulfilled; and identifies the woman as 'the great city which reigns over the kings of the earth,' unmistakably Rome.
